SK2154 The sort has no ordering to use

A sort or ordering falls back to Comparer<T>.Default for a type that implements neither IComparable<T> nor IComparable, and no comparer is passed.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

Comparer<T>.Default throws InvalidOperationException on the first comparison it is asked to make when T implements neither interface. The call compiles cleanly, and it needs two elements to fail — so an empty list and a single-element list both sort successfully, which is what the unit test contains and what production does not.

Example

Instead of:

sealed class Point { public int X; }

var sorted = points.OrderBy(p => p).ToList();

Write:

var sorted = points.OrderBy(p => p.X).ToList();

When it does not fire

⚠ The question is only decidable for a sealed type, and that is the finding rather than a limitation to apologise for. Comparer<T>.Default for an unsealed T builds an ObjectComparer that casts each element to IComparable at run time, so a List<Animal> holding Dog : Animal, IComparable<Dog> sorts correctly even though Animal implements nothing. A non-sealed class therefore cannot be reported without guessing what is in the list. The rule fires only where the element or key type is a struct or a sealed reference type, which is where the runtime type is known to be the static one. ⚠ A type parameter is never reported, for the same reason and more strongly: T in an open generic is substituted at every call site, and IComparable may well be among the substitutions — there is no fact here to check. An interface, object, dynamic and an error type are all silent. ⚠ Enums, string, every primitive, ValueTuple, DateTime, Guid and Nullable<T> over a comparable T all implement one of the two interfaces and are excluded by the check rather than by a list. ⚠ `Queryable` overloads are excluded: an OrderBy that becomes an ORDER BY is ordered by the database and never touches Comparer<T>.Default. ⚠ `hasFix: false`: the repair is either an IComparable<T> implementation or a comparer, and both require knowing what order was wanted — the one thing the source does not say.
